title: Building the Prophet's Mosque
reader_question: How did a yard for drying dates become the Prophet's ﷺ mosque, and who built it?

overview.text: The camel had knelt in a yard where dates were spread out to dry, in the quarter of Banu al-Najjar. Two orphan boys owned it, and some of the Muslims already prayed there in the open. The Prophet ﷺ had no mosque in Madinah yet; he prayed wherever the time of prayer found him. Now he wanted this ground for one. But the yard was crowded with palms, old graves and ruins, and the people he offered to pay had other ideas about its price. Everything would have to be cleared, and built by hand.

account.title: A price no one would take

paragraphs.text: The Prophet ﷺ ordered that a mosque be built there, and sent for the leading men of Banu al-Najjar. When they came, he said: "Banu al-Najjar, name me a price for this walled plot of yours." "No, by Allah," they said. "We seek its price only from Allah."

paragraphs.text: He called the two boys as well, and bargained with them for the yard, so that he could make it a mosque. "No," they said. "We give it to you, Messenger of Allah." Anas, who tells of the clan's answer, says nothing of money changing hands. Other reports remember that the Prophet ﷺ would not take the yard as a gift, and bought it from the two boys. The historian al-Waqidi gives the price as ten dinars, and says Abu Bakr paid it for him.

paragraphs.text: The plot was far from empty. Anas listed what was in it: date palms, the graves of polytheists, and ruins. The Prophet ﷺ ordered the palms cut down, the graves dug up and the ruins levelled. The felled palms were set in a row along the side that faced the qibla, the direction of prayer, and the posts on either side of the doorway were made of stone. The walls would be raised from labin: bricks of clay, dried but not fired.

paragraphs.text: The Prophet ﷺ did not stand and watch. He carried bricks alongside the others. He worked on the mosque himself to make the Muslims eager to work on it, and the Emigrants from Makkah and the Ansar, the Helpers of Madinah, threw themselves into the work. One of the Muslims put it in a line of verse: "If we sit idle while the Prophet works, that would be misguided work on our part." ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib had lines of his own: "Not equal are the one who builds mosques, toiling in them standing and sitting, and the one who keeps away from the dust."

The Prophet ﷺ saw ‘Ammar and began brushing the dust from him. He asked him, "‘Ammar, won't you carry as your companions carry?" "I want the reward from Allah," ‘Ammar replied. As he brushed the dust away, he said: "Woe to ‘Ammar, the rebel party will kill him. He calls them to Paradise, and they call him to the Fire." And ‘Ammar said, "I seek refuge in Allah from trials." Long afterwards, when ‘Ammar was killed at Siffin, ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr reminded his father of those words, and of the day the Messenger of Allah ﷺ built the mosque.

paragraphs.text: The mosque that rose from the yard was simple. In the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar said, it was built of mud brick, roofed with palm fronds, and held up by pillars of palm trunks. Its prayer wall faced Jerusalem: for their first seventeen months in Madinah, Mu‘adh ibn Jabal recalled, the Prophet ﷺ prayed towards it. When the Ansar gathered money and asked him to build it up and adorn it ("How long are we to pray under these palm fronds?"), he answered: "I have no wish to turn away from my brother Moses. A shelter like the shelter of Moses."

in_depth.title: Whose yard was it, and was it bought?

paragraphs.text: The reports name the boys' guardian differently. In Ibn Ishaq's account it is Mu‘adh ibn ‘Afra; in ‘Urwah's report in al-Bukhari, and in al-Zuhri's in al-Bayhaqi, it is As‘ad ibn Zurarah, one of the first of the Ansar to accept Islam. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar names Abu Ayyub. Ibn Hajar judges As‘ad the better-established name, and suggests the boys may have been in more than one man's care, or passed from one guardian to the next after As‘ad.

paragraphs.text: They differ on the price, too. In Anas's report the leading men of Banu al-Najjar refuse any price, and Ibn Hajar notes that the plain sense of his words is that no price was taken; the biographers, he says, report otherwise. In ‘Urwah's report the boys offer the yard as a gift. Al-Zuhri gives three versions without choosing between them: the boys gave it; As‘ad offered them palms of his own in the quarter of Banu Bayadah in exchange; or the Prophet ﷺ bought it from them. Ibn Hajar cites Musa ibn ‘Uqba, from al-Zuhri, for the ten dinars, and al-Waqidi for Abu Bakr paying them. He reconciles the reports this way: when the clan said they sought its price only from Allah, the Prophet ﷺ asked who owned it, they named the two boys, and he bought it from them; those who had refused payment may then have paid the boys on his behalf. Al-Zubayr says Abu Ayyub settled with them.

in_depth.title: A yard, a garden, or both?

paragraphs.text: Anas calls the plot a ha'it, a walled garden, while ‘Urwah calls it a mirbad, a drying yard. Ibn Hajar suggests it had once been a garden that fell to ruin and became a drying yard, which would explain the palms and the ruins in it, or that part was garden and part was yard. One of Anas's transmitters, Hammad ibn Salamah, has "tilled land" where others have "ruins".

in_depth.title: ‘Ammar and the words about his death

paragraphs.text: Al-Bukhari records these words in Abu Sa‘id's report of the building, through ‘Ikrimah: in his chapter on jihad (no. 2812) without any doubt, and in his chapter on mosques (no. 447) in some transmissions of the Sahih (Ibn al-Sakan's and Karimah's) but not in others (Abu Dharr's and al-Asili's). That is why al-Bayhaqi, working from a copy without them, thought al-Bukhari had left the phrase out, perhaps because another student of Abu Sa‘id, Abu Nadrah, placed it at the digging of the Trench, years later; he allows that the Prophet ﷺ may have said it on both occasions. At the battle of Siffin, ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr recalled those words, and the day the mosque was built, when ‘Ammar was killed there.
